sources.citation: Fennell BD, Chavez S, McKay G. Destruction of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances in Reverse Osmosis Concentrate Using UV-Advanced Reduction Processes. ACS ES&T Water. 2024;4(11):4818-4827.

evidence_chunks.text: This study evaluates the effectiveness of the UV/sulfite ARP in reverse osmosis concentrate (ROC) containing high concentrations of dissolved organic carbon, nitrate, and carbonate species.
ROC was spiked with mg/L concentrations of PFOS, PFBS, PFOA, and PFBA to assess PFAS defluorination performance under UV-advanced reduction.
Hardness removal and preoxidation of ROC with UV/persulfate enabled more than 90% PFAS defluorination within 24 h of subsequent UV/sulfite treatment.
Appropriate pretreatment steps increase the effectiveness of PFAS destruction using UV-ARP, supporting application of UV-ARP for PFAS destruction in ROC and other concentrated waste streams.

source_limitations: Only abstract-level information on ROC composition and operating conditions was accessible from the inspected page; detailed energy use and cost data could not be confirmed.
ROC matrix is a specific water reuse concentrate with added PFAS; results may not directly transfer to other RO brines or mixed membrane concentrates.
sources.title: Destruction of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances in Reverse Osmosis Concentrate Using UV-Advanced Reduction Processes

sources.citation: Khodayari E, Juby G, Liu Y, et al. A Bioelectrochemical Approach for Brine Management in Water Reuse Plants: Pilot-Scale Evaluation of Microbial Fuel Cells for RO Concentrate Treatment and CEC and PFAS Removal. Sustainability. 2026;18(9):4540.

evidence_chunks.text: The pilot study evaluated a microbial fuel cell system for treatment of reverse osmosis concentrate generated from a municipal water-reuse pilot train.
Feedwater to the microbial fuel cell system was RO concentrate generated by a UF pretreatment unit and a closed-circuit RO (CCRO) unit.
Detected PFAS in the RO concentrate included PFOS (31.7 ng/L), PFOA (4.6 ng/L), and PFHxA (12.3 ng/L), with other species below reporting limits.
The microbial fuel cell achieved partial removal of selected PFAS from RO concentrate while simultaneously generating electrical power from the concentrate organics.

source_limitations: Full PDF access from the primary MDPI site was rate-limited; quantitative removal percentages for individual PFAS and detailed energy recovery metrics could not all be verified.
Study focuses on one municipal reuse RO concentrate with relatively low ng/L PFAS; applicability to higher-strength concentrates is uncertain.
sources.title: A Bioelectrochemical Approach for Brine Management in Water Reuse Plants: Pilot-Scale Evaluation of Microbial Fuel Cells for RO Concentrate Treatment and CEC and PFAS Removal

sources.citation: Safulko A, Cath TY, Li F, et al. Rejection of Perfluoroalkyl Acids by Nanofiltration and Reverse Osmosis in a High-Recovery Closed-Circuit Membrane Filtration System. Separation and Purification Technology. 2024; in press.

evidence_chunks.text: The rejection of nine PFAAs by four spiral-wound membrane products spanning loose NF to seawater RO was investigated in a pilot-scale closed-circuit membrane filtration system.
Closed-circuit sequences operated up to 97% water recovery, enabling simultaneous investigation of the impact of recovery, that is, PFAA concentration, and ionic strength on separation.
During CCMF sequences to 97% water recovery, NF90, CR100, and SW30 membranes exhibited overall rejection values greater than 98.3% for the PFAAs quantified.
Average PFOS concentrations in the feed-retentate side increased to about 0.132 mg/L at 90% recovery and about 0.382 mg/L at 97% recovery.
Specific energy for 97% recovery experiments ranged from 0.14 kWh/m3 for the loose NF membrane to 0.57 kWh/m3 for the tight RO membrane.

source_limitations: Experiments used dechlorinated tap water spiked with PFAAs rather than real PFAS-impacted groundwaters or wastewaters.
Study quantifies concentration in the feed-retentate but does not follow downstream management or destruction of the generated concentrate.
sources.title: Rejection of Perfluoroalkyl Acids by Nanofiltration and Reverse Osmosis in a High-Recovery Closed-Circuit Membrane Filtration System

sources.citation: American Membrane Technology Association (AMTA). Closed-Circuit High-Pressure Membrane Systems for the Separation of Per and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances. AMTA fact sheet; accessed 2026.

evidence_chunks.text: Four commercially available membranes (NF270, NF90, CR100, and SW30) were investigated for their PFAS rejection performance in a full-scale closed-circuit desalination pilot module.
The pilot module operated at 97% recovery, focusing on removal of perfluoroalkyl acids and standard performance metrics such as conductivity and TOC rejection.
Results indicate that tight NF and RO membranes can be used to concentrate PFAS streams by a factor of 33 at 97% recovery with very low permeate PFAA concentrations.

source_limitations: Fact sheet summarizes a pilot study but provides limited quantitative data on feed and concentrate PFAS concentrations, co-contaminants, and operating pressures.
Energy use, cost analysis, and downstream handling or destruction of the concentrated PFAS waste stream are only qualitatively discussed, if at all.
sources.title: Closed-Circuit High-Pressure Membrane Systems for the Separation of Per and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances

sources.citation: Author(s) not clearly visible. Investigation of PFAS Rejection by Closed-Circuit Reverse Osmosis and Nanofiltration and Sorption to Treatment Materials during Groundwater Treatment: A Pilot Demonstration. Separation and Purification Technology. 2025;377:134308.

evidence_chunks.text: A pilot closed-circuit membrane system operating at recoveries of 80, 85, and 90% treated aqueous film-forming foam impaired groundwater with total PFAS around 14.3 µg/L.
NF rejection ranged from about 97.9 to 99% depending on functional group and chain length, while RO rejection exceeded 99% for all PFAS.
PFOS represented 60–85% of total PFAS sorbed to all treatment materials, with solid-phase PFAS concentration on 0.2 µm filters roughly ten times greater than any other media.

source_limitations: Full text was not accessible from the inspected publisher page; data on concentrate PFAS concentrations, volume reduction factors, and co-contaminant behavior are incomplete.
Downstream handling of PFAS-loaded solids and concentrates is not described in the available abstract; energy and cost data are not reported.
sources.title: Investigation of PFAS Rejection by Closed-Circuit Reverse Osmosis and Nanofiltration and Sorption to Treatment Materials during Groundwater Treatment: A Pilot Demonstration

sources.citation: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation. Enhancing Recovery for Potable Reuse: Pilot Evaluation of Closed Circuit Reverse Osmosis (CCRO) and Forward Osmosis (FO) Alternatives for Concentrate Treatment. Desalination and Water Purification Research Report No. 216. 2022.

evidence_chunks.text: The pilot evaluated CCRO and FO-based alternatives to manage RO concentrate in a potable reuse context, with water quality samples analyzed using EPA Method 537.1 for PFAS.
Sampling included PFAS along with ethylene glycol, semi-volatile organics, and priority pollutants to characterize concentrate and treated streams under different recovery conditions.

source_limitations: The PDF could not be fully rendered by the search tool; only limited methodological text was visible, preventing extraction of detailed PFAS concentration, recovery, and performance data.
Costs, specific energy consumption, and long-term operational behavior of CCRO/FO for PFAS-rich concentrates are not accessible from the inspected excerpts.
sources.title: Desalination and Water Purification Research Report No. 216: Enhancing Recovery for Potable Reuse – Pilot Evaluation of Closed Circuit Reverse Osmosis (CCRO) and Forward Osmosis (FO) Alternatives for Concentrate Treatment

sources.citation: McDonough KM, et al. Validation of supercritical water oxidation to destroy perfluoroalkyl acids. Remediation Journal. 2022;32(3):285–300.

evidence_chunks.text: The study field-validated supercritical water oxidation to treat a concentrated waste stream containing twelve perfluoroalkyl acids.
Liquid and gaseous effluents were characterized following USEPA Method 537.1 and Other Test Method 45 to assess PFAS destruction and potential atmospheric releases.
An appropriate treatment strategy for PFAS-impacted waste includes multiple technologies in series to concentrate PFAS into the smallest possible volume for energy-intensive destruction.

source_limitations: Access to the full text was blocked; quantitative influent and effluent PFAS concentrations, destruction efficiencies, and detailed operating conditions could not be confirmed.
The concentrated PFAS waste stream treated was not explicitly identified as membrane-derived; linkages to RO or NF concentrate management are inferred rather than demonstrated.
sources.title: Validation of Supercritical Water Oxidation to Destroy Perfluoroalkyl Acids

sources.citation: Authors not fully visible. Supercritical Water Oxidation for the Destruction of Spent Media Wastes Generated from PFAS Treatment. Chemosphere. 2024; in press.

evidence_chunks.text: This project is the first study on the use of supercritical water oxidation to destroy both the spent media and the PFAS adsorbed onto it.
Supercritical water oxidation has been previously reported to destroy PFAS in liquid wastes such as aqueous film-forming foams; here it is applied to PFAS captured on spent GAC and AIX.

source_limitations: Only abstract text was accessible; influent PFAS loadings on spent media, destruction efficiencies, and byproduct characterization could not be extracted.
The spent media originate from sorptive treatment, not membranes, but the study informs destruction options for solid PFAS residuals that may arise downstream of membrane concentrates.
sources.title: Supercritical Water Oxidation for the Destruction of Spent Media Wastes Generated from PFAS Treatment

sources.citation: Authors not fully visible. PFOS destruction in a continuous supercritical water oxidation reactor. Chemical Engineering Journal. 2023;

evidence_chunks.text: Technologies such as granular activated carbon, ion exchange resins, foam fractionation, and reverse osmosis separate PFAS but generate concentrated waste streams requiring end-of-life treatment.
Hydrothermal treatment and supercritical water oxidation were investigated as effective destruction technologies for perfluorinated organic molecules including PFOS.

source_limitations: Full text access was blocked; specific PFOS influent concentrations, residence times, energy inputs, and destruction efficiencies could not be captured.
The work uses model PFOS solutions rather than actual RO or NF concentrates; extrapolation to complex membrane brines must be done cautiously.
sources.title: PFOS Destruction in a Continuous Supercritical Water Oxidation Reactor

sources.citation: Ekande OS, et al. Exploring Perfluoroalkyl and Polyfluoroalkyl Substance Presence and Potential Leaching from Reverse Osmosis Membranes: Implications for Drinking Water Treatment. Environmental Science & Technology. 2024;58:15799–15806.

evidence_chunks.text: The presence of PFAS in commercial reverse osmosis membranes was investigated using leaching experiments and a direct total oxidizable precursor assay applied to membrane fragments.
Forty membrane fragments of 1 cm2 were placed into 35 mL of Milli-Q water; after 48 h sonication, PFAS in the leachate were extracted and quantified by LC‑HRMS.
In the leaching experiment, several PFAS, including PFOS and PFOA, were detected in water with surface-normalized loads between about 17 and 38 pg per cm2 of membrane.
Direct TOPA on membrane samples yielded up to sixteen times higher PFOS mass per cm2 compared to simple leaching, indicating substantial precursor or non-leachable PFAS content in the polymer matrix.

evidence_chunks.section: Data analysis and scenario evaluation, P2–P4
evidence_chunks.text: Extrapolating to a 40 m2 element and assuming realistic leaching scenarios, the authors estimated potential ΣPFAS release on the order of tens of milligrams per element over its lifetime.

source_limitations: Study focuses on intact commercial RO elements rather than membranes that have operated on PFAS-impacted water; actual PFAS loads on spent elements may be higher.
Leaching tests used Milli-Q water and accelerated laboratory conditions; real system prewashing, cleaning practices, and concentrate-side exposures are not fully represented.
sources.title: Exploring Perfluoroalkyl and Polyfluoroalkyl Substance Presence and Potential Leaching from Reverse Osmosis Membranes: Implications for Drinking Water Treatment

sources.citation: Huling SG, et al. PFAS Destruction in IX Still Bottoms with Plasma Vortex Technology. Journal and year not fully visible; Drexel University repository record.

evidence_chunks.text: After ion exchange media regeneration with a solvent brine, forty-five liters of a distilled PFAS concentrate, or still bottom, containing approximately 640 mg/L total PFAS was recovered.
The still bottom represented an overall concentration factor of about thirty thousand relative to the original PFAS-containing water.
The treated still bottom was further polished by reverse osmosis, and the RO retentate was returned to the plasma treatment system, forming a closed loop with no liquid discharge.

source_limitations: The concentrate originates from IX regeneration rather than a membrane separation step, but the process demonstrates an integrated loop where RO retentate is recycled into a destructive technology.
Detailed energy consumption for the plasma and RO steps and cost analysis are not available from the inspected record.
sources.title: PFAS Destruction in IX Still Bottoms with Plasma Vortex Technology

sources.citation: Authors not fully visible. PFAS Destruction Using Supercritical Water Oxidation (SCWO) at Peterson Space Force Base. Journal of Environmental Engineering. 2025;

evidence_chunks.text: Supercritical water oxidation was deployed to treat PFAS-impacted aqueous streams at Peterson Space Force Base, with reverse osmosis used upstream to concentrate PFAS and increase SCWO efficiency.
The study notes that concentrating PFAS by reverse osmosis prior to SCWO can reduce overall energy use and reactor volume requirements for destruction.

source_limitations: Only limited abstract-level text was available; specific RO recovery, concentrate factors, PFAS species and concentrations, and SCWO performance metrics are not accessible.
The work focuses on AFFF-impacted waters at a military site; broader applicability to municipal PFAS membrane concentrates is implied but not demonstrated.
sources.title: PFAS Destruction Using Supercritical Water Oxidation (SCWO) at Peterson Space Force Base
